sections.body:
# Draftsman

**Draftsman** is the organisation behind the Tracepaper ecosystem — a collection of tools that transform domain knowledge into executable systems.

Our mission is to make **architectural thinking operational**: helping teams design, evolve, and deploy software that remains explainable over time.  
We combine model-driven design, serverless automation, and visual traceability into one coherent environment.

## Structure
Draftsman operates as a **federated organisation** of focused products:
- **Tracepaper** – for domain modelling and automated code generation.
- **Workbench** – for documentation, shaping, and architectural reasoning.
- **Papers** – for publishing knowledge artefacts and shared principles.

Each product is intentionally independent — both technically and legally — enabling flexible evolution and clear value attribution.

## Vision
Draftsman believes that software architecture should be **composable, transparent, and explainable**.  
Every decision, from a design trade-off to a business rule, should remain traceable from intent to implementation.

We pursue this through:
- Declarative models that describe behaviour, not syntax.
- Reproducible builds and measurable architectural integrity.
- Tight feedback loops between model, runtime, and organisation.

## Governance
Architectural principles and decisions are managed as first-class artefacts.  
Every change is stored, versioned, and reviewable — ensuring accountability without bureaucracy.  
Licensing, billing, and build metrics are coordinated through the Draftsman backend, aligning operational transparency with business clarity.

# Documenting Tracepaper

Tracepaper is rapidly evolving from a prototype into a full-fledged platform. Its architecture is rich — spanning modeler, build agent, backend, and integrations — but that same richness makes it **hard to explain succinctly**.

We need a structured, self-consistent way to **document how Tracepaper works, why it exists, and how all parts connect**. The goal is not to produce traditional documentation, but to make the system *self-describing* — where models, decisions, and principles collectively tell the story.

## The problem
Today, understanding Tracepaper requires traversing multiple mental layers — DSL, architecture, pricing, licensing, and philosophy. These insights live in our heads, microdocs, and Slack threads, but not yet in one navigable form.

This makes it difficult to:
- Onboard contributors or collaborators.
- Communicate Tracepaper’s design philosophy to partners or early adopters.
- Keep architectural intent aligned as the system evolves.

## The idea
Build a **living documentation space** within Workbench that reflects Tracepaper’s inner structure:
- Each decision, principle, and persona becomes a navigable node.
- Visual overviews (C4 + Mermaid) reveal system relationships.
- Contextual references (e.g., license model, AWS architecture) are embedded where relevant.

The output should feel like an **interactive codex**, blending architecture and narrative — something you can *read, explore, or reason through*.

## Appetite
We set an appetite of **six weeks**. The goal is not perfection but coherence: by the end, anyone reading the documentation should understand how Tracepaper fits together and why it was built this way.

## Risks and boundaries
- We deliberately avoid implementing advanced publishing or export features — focus on the internal narrative first.
- The scope is limited to documenting Tracepaper itself, not Draftsman as a whole.

## Success looks like
- Each major subsystem (Modeler, Build Agent, Backend) has a corresponding scope.
- Decisions are linked to principles and personas, forming an explorable web.
- The documentation is understandable without prior context.

> “A reader should be able to start anywhere in the Tracepaper model and end up understanding why it exists.”

graph TD
    A[Tracepaper System] --> B[Modeler]
    A --> C[Build Agent]
    A --> D[Backend]
    B --> E[User Interaction]
    C --> F[Code Generation]
    D --> G[Licensing & Billing]
    E --> H[Documentation Layer]
    H -->|Connects| B
    H -->|Connects| C
    H -->|Connects| D

# Workbench

**Workbench** is the environment where thinking and building converge — a tool for shaping ideas, capturing reasoning, and evolving architecture as living knowledge.

## The problem
Teams accumulate knowledge in disconnected places: design docs, tickets, chat threads, and wikis. None of these stay aligned with the actual architecture. As systems evolve, **context decays** — decisions lose their “why,” and the link between intent and implementation fades.

We need a way to keep architectural intent and project reality in sync — without introducing process overhead.

## The concept
Workbench provides a structured yet flexible way to document **“what is,” “what might be,” and “what is now.”**  
It treats every piece of information — decisions, principles, personas, scopes, and pitches — as **microdocs**: atomic, versioned, and traceable. Together they form a navigable knowledge graph that reflects the organisation’s evolving system landscape.

Workbench is not another note-taking tool. It’s a **thinking surface** for shaping work — one that connects architecture, decision-making, and documentation into a single flow.

## Key ideas
- **Microdocs:** small, atomic documents that represent reasoning rather than prose.
- **Linkability:** every concept (decision, principle, scope) can reference others — forming living architecture.
- **Temporal awareness:** change is not overwritten but **accumulated**, preserving traceability.
- **Shape Up integration:** supports shaping cycles, pitches, and bets natively.

## Appetite
Six weeks to establish the core: editing, linking, and navigating microdocs. This cycle focuses on **structure, navigation, and persistence**, not polish or publishing.

## Boundaries
- No real-time collaboration (out of scope).
- No external sync (e.g., GitHub, Confluence) in this iteration.
- Focus on usability and local persistence first.

## Success looks like
- Users can create, edit, and link microdocs in a coherent workspace.
- Relationships between docs can be visualised (e.g., decision links, scope hierarchy).
- The system feels frictionless — **writing equals modelling.**

> “Workbench captures the thinking that happens between code and conversation — before it’s lost.”

# System setup

The **System setup** scope defines the foundational architecture of the Tracepaper ecosystem — the minimal set of components needed to make the system coherent, deployable, and observable.

It captures all early design decisions that shaped the technical backbone: how components connect, where boundaries lie, and what trade-offs define the platform’s structure.

### Purpose
To establish a consistent baseline across Tracepaper’s modeler, build agent, backend, and supporting infrastructure. This ensures that every product can evolve independently while remaining part of one cohesive ecosystem.

### In scope
- Initial system decomposition (Modeler, Build Agent, Backend, Outbox).
- Communication flows and API contracts.
- Decisions that govern packaging, deployment, and cross-component interaction.
- The principles and constraints that shape each subsystem’s autonomy.

### Out of scope
- Detailed implementation of individual features (e.g., licensing flows, billing UI).
- Runtime operations, monitoring, and cost-optimization work.

### Deliverables
- A documented system map (components, relations, responsibilities).
- Decision records (DD/ADR) explaining key trade-offs.
- Linked principles and personas to provide rationale and context.

### Progress
Current progress: **78.75%** — major decisions and component relationships are defined; refinement and cross-linking are ongoing.

89ebb234-da99-4e5b-ae43-e2739b386925.title: EAP 1: Functional boundaries and organizational flexibility
89ebb234-da99-4e5b-ae43-e2739b386925.principle:
### Statement
To ensure long-term resilience and independence, we design products around **clear functional and organizational boundaries**.
Each product in the Draftsman ecosystem (e.g. Tracepaper, Workbench) operates as a standalone system with its own runtime, licensing model, and commercial identity.

### Rationale
This separation limits systemic risk and prevents cross-product coupling — both technically and commercially. By keeping products fully autonomous, we preserve the ability to evolve, pause, or transfer them independently, without affecting the rest of the portfolio.

Even shared infrastructure such as licensing, authentication, or billing is implemented **per product**, not centrally. Only truly external services (e.g. Stripe for payments) are cross-cutting, and even then isolated by environment and catalog.

This approach means we cannot easily bundle products commercially — for example, offering joint discounts or shared entitlements. To compensate, each product must be **competitively priced on its own merits**.

> Example: Tracepaper and Workbench each operate their own license server, reflecting distinct license semantics and deployment models. If one product is discontinued or sold, the other continues unaffected.

### Implication / Acceptance
We accept that architectural independence comes at the cost of commercial integration. However, it also ensures clean handovers, reduced blast radius, and optional separation into distinct legal entities when needed (e.g. risk management or IP transfer).

> Example: if a product reaches end-of-life but retains value for others, it can be sold or open-sourced without disrupting the rest of the ecosystem.

a201f648-b359-4621-b45c-8ea40b4d76e3.title: EAP 2: We prefer serverless technologies
a201f648-b359-4621-b45c-8ea40b4d76e3.principle:
### Statement
To maximize focus on domain logic and reduce operational burden, we **prefer serverless technologies** for all Draftsman products.
Each product is designed as a standalone system that leverages managed cloud services whenever possible.

### Rationale
Serverless platforms (such as AWS Lambda, DynamoDB, and AppSync) allow small teams to operate at scale without managing infrastructure. This choice aligns with our goal of maintaining functional independence across products, while ensuring operational consistency and predictable cost structures.

By avoiding persistent infrastructure, we also reduce the blast radius of change: every deployment is ephemeral, traceable, and fully reproducible.

This architectural stance supports our lean organizational model — no central DevOps team, minimal cloud footprint, and direct ownership of runtime behaviour within each product.

### Implication / Acceptance
We accept that this preference limits portability and deep customization. Certain use cases (e.g. heavy compute, long-running processes, or specific integrations) may not fit within a serverless boundary.

In such cases, exceptions must be explicitly justified, and isolation maintained to prevent drift from the overall deployment model.

> Example: Tracepaper’s Build Agent is fully serverless by design, translating models into deployable AWS SAM stacks. Future products may adopt containerized alternatives, but only if they preserve the same hands-off operational characteristics.

f7031fcf-142e-4ed2-bf1a-92a192da5f93.title: Decision 1: Introduction of Tracepaper

sections.body:
# Problem statement

Within Draftsman we identified the need for a platform that not only documents domain models, but also translates them directly into production-ready software.

Existing low-code platforms often obscure the underlying architecture, limit extensibility, and impose their own opinions on hosting and integration. This conflicts with our goal to make **software architecture explicit and inspectable**—not hidden behind black boxes.

We therefore looked for a way to make our **vision of model-driven development** tangible in our own product.

# Decision

We introduce a new software system: **Tracepaper**. It becomes our primary instrument to realize model-driven development within the Draftsman ecosystem.

Tracepaper combines:
- A visual modeling tool for capturing domain concepts such as commands, aggregates, views, projections, and notifiers.
- A code generator that transforms these models into production-ready AWS Serverless components.

With this decision we establish the foundation for a platform that narrows the gap between **architecture and execution**.

### Considerations
Alternatives such as commercial low-code tools (e.g. OutSystems, Mendix, Camunda) offer speed but limit control and transparency. A fully manual approach, on the other hand, makes rapid iteration impossible. Tracepaper positions itself in between: **full control where it matters, automation where it helps.**

### Expected impact
- **Architectural:** Tracepaper becomes a new core system within the Draftsman landscape.
- **Organizational:** Facilitates knowledge sharing and repeatable architectural decisions.
- **Technical:** Establishes the basis for future products built on the same principles.

f7031fcf-142e-4ed2-bf1a-92a192da5f93.decision: We introduce a new system, Tracepaper, to realize our vision of model-driven development within the Draftsman ecosystem.

sections.body:
# Problem statement

After introducing Tracepaper as a system, we need a way to **automatically translate the modeled domain logic into executable software**.

The purpose of Tracepaper is to bridge the gap between conceptual modeling (commands, aggregates, views, projections, notifiers) and a distributed runtime. In practice, this means that generated applications must run on **AWS Serverless**, using components such as Lambda, DynamoDB, S3, and AppSync.

Writing this code manually is time-consuming and error-prone. Much of the infrastructure code (IaC, deployment configuration, boilerplate) repeats across projects. We therefore seek to **automate this translation**, without sacrificing transparency of the generated code.

# Decision

We build a **code generator** that translates Tracepaper DSL models into production-ready application code and infrastructure (IaC) for AWS Serverless.

This generator acts as the bridge between conceptual models and executable reality. The build process is executed by a dedicated component — the **Build Agent** — responsible for receiving ZIP files with model data, generating code, and publishing the results.

The generator is implemented in **Python**, using **AWS SAM** for infrastructure definition and packaging.

### Considerations
- **Alternative 1:** Manual code generation via templates inside the modeler — too limited and lacks lifecycle control.  
- **Alternative 2:** External build services (e.g. CloudBuild, CodePipeline) — add dependencies and reduce flexibility.

A custom generator provides the best balance of control, speed, and extensibility. It also allows support for **additional generation engines** in the future (e.g. container-based or on-premise deployments).

### Expected impact
- **Architectural:** The Build Agent becomes a core component within Tracepaper.  
- **Technical:** Code generation and IaC are standardized; build outputs are reproducible.  
- **Strategic:** Tracepaper differentiates itself from conventional low-code platforms by providing **full transparency of generated code**.

effect.description: Code generator for transforming models into AWS Serverless artifacts.

ystatement.context: Within Tracepaper, which aims to transform domain models into executable software on AWS Serverless.
ystatement.concern: Manual translation of DSL models into executable code is error-prone, inconsistent, and time-consuming.
ystatement.decision: We build a code generator in Python that translates Tracepaper models into production-ready AWS Serverless code and IaC via AWS SAM.
ystatement.alternatives: Manual generation through modeler templates, or relying on external build services such as CloudBuild or CodePipeline.
ystatement.quality: Standardization, transparency, and higher development speed without losing control over generated code.
ystatement.consequence: The Build Agent becomes a central component within Tracepaper, managing the entire build and generation pipeline.

sections.body:
# Problem statement

The first versions of Tracepaper (v0–v4) ran entirely in the browser. While this provided a low entry barrier, it led to limitations in **performance**, **file access**, and **user experience**.

Browser-based models required complex workarounds such as IndexedDB, Web Workers, and simulated file systems. Offline editing was difficult, and larger projects (hundreds of XML or JSON models) could noticeably slow down the UI.

We want to create an environment that feels like a **true IDE**—fast, robust, and integrated with local developer tools such as Git, the AWS CLI, and external editors. This requires a shift from a web-first approach to a **desktop-native experience**.

# Decision

We develop a **desktop version of the Tracepaper Modeler**, built with **PyWebView** and **Alpine.js**.

This choice enables:
- Direct access to local file structures and repositories without browser sandbox restrictions.
- A smooth, native-like user experience.
- Offline editing without dependency on a browser cache or remote server.

The desktop modeler retains the modern web-based UI (HTML, Tailwind, Alpine.js) while running inside a lightweight desktop container with a **local Python backend**.

### Considerations
- **Alternative 1:** Improve the web version (Tracepaper 4) using PWA techniques → remained slow for large models and limited in file access.
- **Alternative 2:** Build a fully native GUI using Qt or Electron → higher development and maintenance cost, loss of existing frontend reuse.

PyWebView offers the best of both worlds: web technology with native integration, lightweight and cross-platform.

### Expected impact
- **User experience:** faster loading times, smoother editor performance, native look & feel.  
- **Architectural:** the modeler becomes a standalone container within Tracepaper, separated from the Build Agent and backend.  
- **Strategic:** a desktop version makes Tracepaper more appealing to professional users expecting IDE-grade tooling.

ystatement.context: Within Tracepaper, earlier web-based versions (v0–v4) suffered from performance, file-access, and UX constraints.
ystatement.concern: Browser limitations hindered scalability, offline editing, and integration with local developer workflows.
ystatement.decision: We build a desktop modeler using PyWebView and Alpine.js to deliver native performance and local integration while retaining web-based flexibility.
ystatement.alternatives: Improve the existing web PWA or build a fully native GUI using frameworks such as Qt or Electron.
ystatement.quality: Fast, reliable, cross-platform experience with minimal maintenance overhead.
ystatement.consequence: The modeler becomes a standalone container, decoupled from the Build Agent and backend, forming the user-facing core of Tracepaper.

df4dba93-2e4c-4b69-bb84-1d4579493641.title: Decision 4: Introduce a ZIP-based API for the Build Agent

sections.body:
# Problem statement

Now that the **Build Agent** is designed as a standalone, serverless component responsible for code generation, a reliable and efficient way is needed to deliver model projects from the **Desktop Modeler**.

A project typically consists of dozens or hundreds of JSON or XML files forming the domain description. Sending these individually through API calls would result in excessive network traffic, complex error handling, and high latency.

We therefore need a **standardized, stateless interface** that allows complete projects to be transferred in a single request, without persistent sessions or long-lived storage.

# Decision

We introduce a **ZIP-based API** as the primary submission mechanism for the Build Agent.

The **Desktop Modeler** bundles all model files into a ZIP archive and sends it via **HTTP POST** to an **AWS Lambda** that serves as the Build Agent entrypoint.

The Lambda:
1. Extracts the ZIP archive into a temporary directory;  
2. Starts the code generation process with the provided metadata;  
3. Uploads the resulting artifacts to an S3 bucket for further processing.

This design ensures that the Build Agent:
- Operates **statelessly** (no session or local storage);  
- Scales horizontally via parallel Lambda invocations;  
- Remains **robust** for large projects with many files.

### Considerations
- **Alternative 1:** Upload individual files to S3 with event triggers → complex orchestration, higher error surface.  
- **Alternative 2:** REST API with per-file requests → too slow and unsuitable for large projects.  

The ZIP-based approach provides simplicity, repeatability, and high throughput with minimal operational overhead.

### Expected impact
- **Architectural:** The Build Agent gains a clear, single entrypoint for build requests.  
- **Technical:** Complete projects can be processed atomically in one transaction.  
- **Security:** Temporary storage minimizes exposure of model data.

effect.description: Stateless entrypoint for model uploads and code generation

ystatement.context: Within Tracepaper, the Build Agent is a serverless component responsible for translating uploaded model projects into executable code.
ystatement.concern: Uploading individual model files creates high network overhead, complexity, and poor scalability for large projects.
ystatement.decision: We introduce a ZIP-based API where the Desktop Modeler sends the complete project archive to a Lambda entrypoint that unpacks, processes, and publishes results.
ystatement.alternatives: Uploading individual files to S3 with triggers, or exposing a REST endpoint for per-file uploads.
ystatement.quality: Stateless design, reproducible builds, and scalable execution with minimal latency.
ystatement.consequence: The Build Agent now exposes a single, efficient entrypoint that simplifies orchestration and reduces operational complexity.

1c9f5c4d-e848-4191-87a2-d40bae96b150.title: Decision 5: Link the Modeler to the Build Agent

sections.body:
# Problem statement

With the **ZIP-based API** now available in the Build Agent, there is a scalable and stateless way to process model projects. The next step is to let the **Desktop Modeler** communicate directly with this API.

The Modeler serves as the development environment where users assemble their domain models. For a seamless workflow, the Modeler must be able to initiate a build request without manual export or upload steps.

A direct connection between the Modeler and Build Agent is essential to:
- shorten the feedback loop;
- trigger builds with a single action;
- ensure consistency between local models and generated output.

1c9f5c4d-e848-4191-87a2-d40bae96b150.decision: The Desktop Modeler connects directly to the Build Agent using the ZIP-based API for one-click, automated builds.

b3923e5a-a3c5-4167-831e-004915ac011f.title: Decision 6: Add an Outbox bucket for artifact storage

sections.body:
# Problem statement

Now that the **Build Agent** can execute builds and generate results, a reliable way is needed to store and expose these output files (artifacts).

A build may produce multiple files — generated code, configuration, metadata — which together exceed Lambda’s 6 MB response limit. Returning them directly over HTTP is therefore infeasible for production use.

We need an **asynchronous, scalable storage mechanism** where build results can be temporarily persisted, so that the Modeler and backend can later retrieve them securely.

# Decision

We introduce an **S3-based Outbox** for storing build artifacts.

After completing a build, the **Build Agent** uploads all generated files to this bucket. The backend or Modeler can then download them through **presigned URLs** with limited lifetime.

This design decouples build execution from result delivery, improving scalability, reliability, and maintainability.

### Trade-offs
- **Alternative 1:** Return build results in HTTP response → unreliable and limited by payload size.  
- **Alternative 2:** Use external storage services (e.g. Cloudflare R2, Dropbox) → adds dependencies and latency.

S3 provides native integration, low cost, and strong durability. Using presigned URLs ensures temporary, secure, and auditable access.

b3923e5a-a3c5-4167-831e-004915ac011f.decision: We add an S3-based Outbox bucket to store build artifacts and deliver them via temporary presigned URLs.

effect.description: Artifact repository for generated build outputs

4ecc5f72-b895-4048-9172-bf823f0b1b7a.title: Decision 7: Link the Build Agent to the Outbox

sections.body:
# Problem statement

After introducing the **Outbox** as the central artifact storage, the next step is to connect the **Build Agent** directly to it.

The Build Agent generates multiple output files after each build, but without automatic publication, users would still need to manually retrieve them — leading to delays and inconsistencies.

To make the build process fully automated, the Build Agent must **upload its results directly** to the Outbox once a build completes.

# Decision

The **Build Agent** is connected to the **Outbox**, ensuring all build artifacts are automatically uploaded to S3 upon completion.

The process works as follows:
1. After a build finishes, the Build Agent bundles the output into a ZIP archive;  
2. A **presigned upload URL** is generated via the backend or AWS SDK;  
3. The ZIP is uploaded directly to the Outbox;  
4. The resulting link is stored in the build metadata.

This integration makes the system fully autonomous, eliminating manual downloads or extra API layers.

### Trade-offs
- **Alternative 1:** Upload via backend → adds latency and compute overhead.  
- **Alternative 2:** Store artifacts in DynamoDB or custom blob storage → unsuitable for binary files.

A direct S3 link offers simplicity, scalability, and security through temporary credentials.

4ecc5f72-b895-4048-9172-bf823f0b1b7a.decision: The Build Agent automatically uploads all generated artifacts to the Outbox via a presigned S3 upload URL.

849de746-95e0-4fee-9c4a-6bd625987833.title: Decision 8: Link the Modeler to the Outbox

sections.body:
# Problem statement

With the **Outbox** now acting as central artifact storage and the **Build Agent** already connected, build artifacts are automatically published. The missing link is between the **Desktop Modeler** and the Outbox, allowing users to easily retrieve their build results.

Without this connection, users must manually open presigned URLs or use external tools to download their files. This is cumbersome, error-prone, and limits the user experience.

To close the feedback loop, the Modeler should provide a **seamless way** to download generated artifacts directly from within the application.

# Decision

We link the **Desktop Modeler** directly to the **Outbox**, allowing users to download build artifacts immediately after a build.

After a build completes:
1. The Build Agent registers the artifact’s location in the backend;  
2. The backend provides the Modeler with a **presigned download URL**;  
3. The user can download or open the file with a single click;  
4. The download occurs directly via S3, without passing through the backend.

This architecture fully closes the build cycle — from model to artifact — in a single integrated flow.

### Trade-offs
- **Alternative 1:** Stream files through the backend → slower and more costly.  
- **Alternative 2:** Manual download via browser or CLI → poor UX and unreliable when URLs expire.

A direct S3 connection via presigned URLs provides maximum speed, safety, and simplicity.

849de746-95e0-4fee-9c4a-6bd625987833.decision: The Desktop Modeler connects directly to the Outbox, allowing one-click artifact downloads via presigned S3 URLs.

9286b792-bbd2-445a-b609-22a5758624c5.title: Decision 9: Introduce the License Management Backend

sections.body:
# Problem statement

Now that the build chain (**Modeler → Build Agent → Outbox**) is fully operational, we need a central service that manages **licensing, usage, and operational visibility**.

While these components together enable an automated flow from model to code, they still lack an **authoritative system of record** that governs who is allowed to build, how usage is measured, and how deployments are monitored across environments.

Additionally, we want Tracepaper to offer users insights into their **runtime resources** — Lambdas, DynamoDB tables, AppSync APIs, Cognito pools, and pipelines — directly from within the Modeler.

To achieve this, we require a new internal component that unifies license management, usage tracking, and operational awareness.

# Decision

We introduce a new **backend service** within Tracepaper called **License Management**.

This backend fulfills four core responsibilities:

1. **License & seat management** — Verifies which users and machines are authorized to execute builds.  
2. **Usage tracking** — Logs the number of Commands, Views, and Notifiers used per build for billing and analytics.  
3. **Pipeline & deployment registry** — When a build is deployed to AWS, a callback to this service records its operational state.  
4. **Modeler integration** — The Modeler retrieves metadata and direct AWS links (pipelines, QA reports, Lambdas, Cognito, etc.) via this backend.

This component becomes the **central administrative layer** of Tracepaper — the junction where model, build, and runtime meet.

### Trade-offs
- **Alternative 1:** Local management in the Modeler → unreliable and hard to synchronize.  
- **Alternative 2:** Third-party licensing service → lacks domain-specific logic for Tracepaper builds and usage metering.

Owning this backend provides full control, better observability, and extensibility for future pricing or compliance features.

effect.description: Backend for licensing, metering, and operational visibility

ystatement.context: Within the Tracepaper ecosystem, which connects model, build, and runtime components.
ystatement.concern: There is no single authoritative service managing licensing, usage metering, or operational visibility across builds and deployments.
ystatement.decision: We introduce a new backend component — License Management — as the administrative core for Tracepaper.
ystatement.alternatives: Handle licenses locally within the Modeler, or delegate management to an external third-party service.
ystatement.quality: Unified control, auditability, and extensibility for future billing, analytics, and compliance.
ystatement.consequence: Tracepaper gains a centralized backend that authorizes builds, tracks usage, and integrates runtime awareness, completing the architectural foundation of the ecosystem.

e78a618d-9cbd-4262-a3dd-177fc80a722f.title: Decision 10: Connect the Desktop Modeler to the License Management Backend

sections.body:
# Problem statement

With the introduction of the **License Management Backend**, Tracepaper now has the infrastructure to centrally manage licensing, usage, and pipelines. To leverage this, the **Desktop Modeler** must communicate directly with that backend.

The Modeler is the user’s main entry point — where builds are triggered, licenses are validated, and projects are managed. Without backend integration it cannot display license status, obtain build tokens, or show linked AWS pipelines and deployments.

A direct API connection is required to provide a consistent and reliable experience across all components.

# Decision

The **Desktop Modeler** connects to the **License Management Backend** through a REST API.

When a project is opened:
1. The Modeler validates the local license with the backend.  
2. It requests a temporary **build token** used for communication with the Build Agent.  
3. It synchronizes usage data (Commands, Read Models, Notifiers) for monthly metering.  
4. It retrieves contextual information about linked pipelines and deployments, exposing relevant **AWS links** in the UI.

This integration makes the Modeler not only a modeling environment but also the hub where **status, licensing, and operational context converge**.

### Trade-offs
- **Alternative 1:** Validate licenses offline → unreliable and prone to abuse.  
- **Alternative 2:** Require users to log in to a separate portal → fragmented workflow and poorer UX.

A direct API integration offers the fastest and most seamless connection between user, model, and backend.

### Expected impact
- **UX:** Real-time license status and direct access to AWS pipelines and deployments.  
- **Architectural:** The Modeler becomes the first client of the License Management Backend.  
- **Security:** All communication uses short-lived tokens over TLS.  
- **Operational:** Builds and usage metrics are synchronized automatically.

e78a618d-9cbd-4262-a3dd-177fc80a722f.decision: The Desktop Modeler integrates directly with the License Management Backend via REST API for license validation, usage synchronization, and operational visibility.

d0a780bd-0b27-4b05-aa71-8e2dc455bc6c.title: Decision 11: Connect the Build Agent to the License Management Backend

sections.body:
# Problem statement

With the **License Management Backend** now operational and responsible for license validation, usage tracking, and pipeline administration, the **Build Agent** must be able to report its build data to it.

Each build contains valuable metadata — start and end time, resources used, build status, project ID, and feature counts (commands, read models, notifiers). Without central registration, these details remain scattered, preventing accurate usage reporting and license compliance monitoring.

It is also essential that the backend knows **which builds are active** and **how often** each user invokes the Build Agent, to enable usage-based billing, debugging, and quality analysis.

# Decision

The **Build Agent** connects to the **License Management Backend** and reports relevant **build metrics** after each build.

The process is as follows:
1. The Build Agent receives a temporary **build token** from the Modeler.  
2. After completing a build, it sends a **metrics payload** to the backend through a secure API call.  
3. The backend records this data in its usage registry, linking it to the corresponding license and pipeline.  
4. Any quota violations or errors are reported back to the Modeler.

The backend processes these metrics for billing, analysis, and operational monitoring.

### Trade-offs
- **Alternative 1:** Store metrics in S3 or local logs → no real-time insight and no license linkage.  
- **Alternative 2:** Periodic synchronization by the Modeler → delayed data, inconsistency, and added complexity.

A direct connection between Build Agent and backend ensures **real-time visibility, simple billing integration, and consistent monitoring**.

### Expected impact
- **Architectural:** The Build Agent becomes a data-producer for the License Management API.  
- **Operational:** Metrics are stored centrally for validation and billing.  
- **UX:** Build history and usage statistics become visible within the Modeler.  
- **Security:** Communication uses short-lived tokens over TLS-secured endpoints.

d0a780bd-0b27-4b05-aa71-8e2dc455bc6c.decision: The Build Agent reports build metrics in real time to the License Management Backend for usage tracking, license validation, and operational insight.

faf777f8-112d-4c6a-9e74-d95b323f68b3.title: Decision 12: Select Stripe as Payment Processor for Professional Licenses

sections.body:
# Problem statement

The **License Management Backend** manages all licenses and usage data for Tracepaper projects. Three license types exist:
- **Personal:** free, limited quota.  
- **Non-profit:** free, higher quota, manual approval.  
- **Professional:** commercial, with paid subscriptions and usage-based billing.

To automatically invoice Professional licenses and securely process payments, an integrated payment platform is required. This platform must combine recurring subscriptions with metered usage (e.g., per Command, Read Model, or Notifier) and support global payments.

Building an in-house payment system would add high operational and compliance costs (PCI-DSS, fraud detection, multi-currency handling). Therefore, integration with a third-party payment processor is necessary.

# Decision

We select **Stripe** as the external payment processor for **Professional licenses**.

Only projects with a Professional license are registered in Stripe. Personal and Non-profit licenses remain free and untracked.

Integration flow:
1. When a Professional license is activated, the backend creates a **Stripe Customer** linked to the project ID and Git repository.  
2. Usage data (commands, read models, notifiers, builds) is periodically sent to **Stripe Usage Records**.  
3. Stripe automatically generates a monthly invoice combining base license fees and metered usage.  
4. Payment and subscription statuses are reported back to the backend via **webhooks**.

### Trade-offs
- **Alternative 1:** Build our own billing system → high complexity and compliance risk.  
- **Alternative 2:** Use simpler platforms (Paddle, Lemon Squeezy) → limited metered billing and seat management support.

Stripe offers the best balance of **flexibility, reliability, and global reach**, enabling seamless coexistence of free and paid licenses.

### Expected impact
- **Architectural:** External payment system integrated for commercial licenses only.  
- **Operational:** Automated billing and invoicing for Professional users.  
- **Commercial:** Personal and Non-profit tiers remain free.  
- **Security:** Stripe ensures PCI-DSS compliance, reducing internal liability.

ystatement.context: Tracepaper’s License Management Backend requires a reliable mechanism to handle paid Professional licenses with metered usage.
ystatement.concern: Internal billing would be costly and non-compliant with PCI-DSS; simpler third-party tools lack metered usage and seat-based billing capabilities.
ystatement.decision: Integrate Stripe as the external payment processor for Professional licenses, handling subscriptions, metering, and invoices.
ystatement.alternatives: Build an in-house billing system; use Paddle or Lemon Squeezy for simplified subscriptions.
ystatement.quality: Security, compliance, and operational scalability with minimal internal complexity.
ystatement.consequence: Stripe becomes the authoritative billing system for Professional users, enabling automated payments while maintaining separation between free and paid license tiers.

4adeb822-c309-49f6-847c-6ed1d111e91d.title: Decision 13: Koppel de License Management-backend aan Stripe

sections.body:
# Probleemstelling

Na de keuze voor **Stripe** als betalingsverwerker (zie Decision 12) moet de **License Management-backend** zorgen voor een betrouwbare synchronisatie tussen het interne licentiesysteem en de externe facturatie.

De backend is de **enige bron van waarheid** voor licentiestatus, usage-statistieken en seat-registratie. Stripe fungeert uitsluitend als uitvoerend facturatieplatform. Zonder automatische synchronisatie zou het risico ontstaan dat verlopen licenties actief blijven of dat gebruik niet correct wordt afgerekend.

Daarnaast moet usage-data actueel blijven, zonder dat gebruikers daarvoor hoeven te wachten of handmatig actie ondernemen. Build-gebeurtenissen moeten direct geregistreerd worden, terwijl overige usage (commands, views, notifiers, etc.) periodiek kan worden bijgewerkt.

# Beslissing

De **License Management-backend** integreert met **Stripe** via een gecontroleerde, backend-gedreven koppeling.

### Synchronisatiefrequentie
1. **Dagelijks** controleert de backend bij Stripe of alle actieve licenties nog geldig zijn en worden betalingen of schorsingen verwerkt.
2. Tijdens diezelfde taak worden de actuele usage-gegevens naar Stripe geüpload als **Usage Records** voor facturatie.
3. **Build-ticks** (het aantal builds per project) worden **event-based** direct naar Stripe gestuurd zodra een build is voltooid, om realtime-accuratesse te behouden.

Stripe verwerkt deze usage-records en genereert maandelijks facturen. De backend blijft leidend in alle beslissingen over licentie-status, activatie en validatie.

### Afweging
- **Alternatief 1:** Webhook-gedreven model → verhoogt complexiteit en maakt de backend afhankelijk van externe triggers.
- **Alternatief 2:** Handmatige synchronisatie → foutgevoelig en niet betrouwbaar op schaal.

Een backend-gedreven, dagelijkse synchronisatie biedt **volledige controle**, **minimale afhankelijkheden** en **betere audit-traceerbaarheid**.

### Verwachte impact
- **Architecturaal:** Stripe wordt een passieve facturatie-endpoint, volledig bestuurd door de backend.
- **Operationeel:** Dagelijkse validatie voorkomt verlopen of foutieve licenties.
- **Realtime-component:** Builds worden direct geregistreerd, zodat het dashboard actueel blijft.
- **Beveiliging:** Alleen uitgaande communicatie met Stripe; geen inkomende webhooks of trust-assumpties.

4adeb822-c309-49f6-847c-6ed1d111e91d.decision: De License Management-backend voert dagelijks een synchronisatie met Stripe uit voor licentievalidatie en usage-registratie, met event-based updates voor builds.

89bf2d4c-b38f-46da-b623-51f4c5cf9c03.title: SAP 1: Tracepaper-systemen zijn modulair ontworpen
89bf2d4c-b38f-46da-b623-51f4c5cf9c03.principle:
### Statement
To ensure **clear separation of responsibility**, all Tracepaper subsystems are designed as **independent, composable modules**.

Each module exposes a minimal, stable interface and avoids shared state, enabling flexible deployment and independent evolution.

### Rationale
This modularity allows Tracepaper to evolve without tight coupling between components such as the Desktop Modeler, Build Agent, and License Management backend.
It supports both **technical isolation** (different technologies, runtimes, or release cycles) and **organizational isolation** (different ownership, or even legal entities if needed).

This approach also makes it easier to test and deploy subsystems individually, keeping the overall system maintainable and resilient to change.

### Implication / Acceptance
We accept that cross-module features (for example, direct data access between the Modeler and Build Agent) must be implemented through **explicit APIs** or **message passing**.
This increases the coordination overhead but preserves long-term stability.

We also accept that user experience improvements requiring deeper integration will need **careful orchestration**, rather than shortcut coupling.

17807819-9e47-4237-ae66-528ad580affe.title: CAP 1: Build Agent werkt stateless en idempotent
17807819-9e47-4237-ae66-528ad580affe.principle:
### Statement
To ensure **deterministic and reproducible builds**, the Build Agent operates as a **stateless, idempotent component**.
Each build request contains all required context (model, configuration, and license token), allowing the agent to process it without relying on prior executions.

### Rationale
Statelessness simplifies scaling and isolation. Multiple build requests can be executed in parallel or retried without side effects. This design minimizes risk of corruption or dependency between builds and aligns with the serverless nature of Tracepaper’s runtime.

An idempotent build process ensures that rerunning a build with the same inputs always produces the same output — a key requirement for traceability, licensing, and reproducibility.

### Implication / Acceptance
We accept that the Build Agent **does not retain local caches or intermediate state** across builds. Any persistent output (e.g. generated artifacts, logs) must be stored externally, typically in the S3-based Outbox.

We also accept that stateful optimizations (like incremental builds or dependency caching) can only be introduced when they are **deterministically reconstructible** from input data or versioned storage.

This design favors **reliability and auditability** over raw build performance.

sections.body:
# The Modeler

**Role summary**
The Modeler is responsible for translating business intent into executable domain models within Tracepaper. They operate at the intersection of business analysis and software design, using visual modeling rather than source code.

**Motivation**
They want to capture complex processes and domain logic quickly — without depending on a full engineering team for every change. Transparency and traceability are essential; they expect the generated code to be production-ready but understandable.

**Goals**
- Express intent through Commands, Aggregates, and Views.
- Validate design decisions visually before implementation.
- Generate deployable serverless systems without writing infrastructure code.

**Frustrations**
- Manual deployment steps or unclear runtime behavior.
- Hidden automation or ‘black box’ low-code platforms.

**Collaboration context**
Modelers often collaborate with Architects and Developers to refine domain boundaries and optimize build configurations. They work closely with the Build Agent through the Desktop Modeler to trigger builds and inspect generated artifacts.

**Example quote**
> “I want to design the behavior once — and know that what goes to production truly matches my model.”

effect.name: Modeler
effect.description: Business-oriented developer or domain designer responsible for authoring Tracepaper models.

ef31a1f4-1740-4081-aaa0-432ce64cdc6c.title: Decision 14: Introduce PyWebview/Flask host for the Desktop Modeler

sections.body:
# Problem statement

To provide a seamless user experience, the Tracepaper Modeler needs a **desktop runtime** that behaves like a native application but reuses existing web components.

Previous browser-based versions (Tracepaper 2–4) relied on PWAs and local storage, but they lacked deep system integration (file access, Git operations, local caching) and suffered from browser sandbox restrictions.

We need a host layer that can:
- Serve the local web UI with full offline support.
- Expose backend functionality (file I/O, ZIP processing, Git, AWS presigned uploads) to the UI.
- Keep the UX lightweight and responsive without bundling a full browser engine like Electron.

# Decision

We introduce a **Webview Host** implemented with **PyWebview** and **Flask**.

Flask provides a lightweight local API server, while PyWebview renders the Alpine.js/DaisyUI interface in a native window. This combination allows us to reuse the same HTML/JS assets across all platforms (macOS, Windows, Linux) and expose controlled Python endpoints to the UI layer.

### Alternatives considered
- **Electron** – powerful, but heavy; adds ~150 MB runtime overhead.
- **Tauri** – leaner, but Rust-based; increases build complexity.

PyWebview/Flask offers the right balance between control, portability, and simplicity while keeping the stack consistent with other Python-based components (e.g., the Build Agent).

ef31a1f4-1740-4081-aaa0-432ce64cdc6c.decision: Use PyWebview with Flask as the desktop host bridge to expose local functionality and render the web-based Modeler UI natively.

effect.label: uses
effect.description: GUI bridge between the frontend and local backend.

c262d374-0b09-4049-937f-f7b1be4de5bb.title: Decision 15: Define interaction between the Modeler persona and the Desktop Modeler

sections.body:
# Problem statement

The **Modeler** persona designs and validates domain models through the Tracepaper interface. For this role, the modeling experience must feel **direct, responsive, and transparent**, without exposing unnecessary technical complexity.

While the PyWebview/Flask-based Desktop Modeler (Decision 14) provides the technical foundation for this, the user interaction model — how Modelers create, inspect, and build — still needed to be defined.

The challenge is to balance **autonomy** (users can model and build without technical barriers) with **safety and control** (respecting licensing, usage metrics, and build isolation).

# Decision

We define the **Modeler-to-Desktop Modeler interaction** as a lightweight client–host relationship.

The Modeler persona interacts exclusively through the UI layer (Alpine.js + DaisyUI) within the PyWebview window. All backend operations — such as opening projects, initiating builds, or retrieving artifacts — are handled via Flask endpoints that expose local functionality.

This design allows Modelers to:
- Work fully offline with locally cached model data.
- Trigger builds via a single command that securely communicates with the Build Agent.
- View build results, logs, and links (e.g. AWS Pipeline, Outbox) without leaving the Modeler environment.

### Alternatives considered
- **Web-only Modeler (PWA)** – insufficient system access and poor offline support.
- **Full Electron shell** – unnecessary runtime weight and duplication of existing web logic.

The chosen approach enables a **coherent and extensible UX** while maintaining a lightweight footprint.

c262d374-0b09-4049-937f-f7b1be4de5bb.decision: The Modeler interacts with the Desktop Modeler through a PyWebview-based host layer, combining local control with a lightweight web UI for a transparent, offline-first modeling experience.
